facts.text: A change to Australian investor tax rebates left Turkey Shoot short of cash, so director Brian Trenchard-Smith had to squeeze a planned 44-day shoot into 28 ten-hour days.
With the schedule slashed, the script shrank by about a quarter, and director Brian Trenchard-Smith improvised action on set because the production couldn't afford to pay stuntmen.
Director Brian Trenchard-Smith described his film as '1984 meets The Camp on Blood Island where they play The Most Dangerous Game.'

The camp's full name in the film is the 'B.F. Skinner Re-Education and Behavior Modification Camp', a nod to the famed behaviorist psychologist. Its sadistic boss is named Thatcher as a political jab.
The camp set was built to hold 500 extras. The budget covered only 75 on the biggest day, so Brian Trenchard-Smith stretched a few dozen to fill the frame.
The first script draft was set in the Depression-era Deep South: 70 pages of chain-gang movie and only 35 of manhunt. Tax financing required an Australian setting, so the story moved to the future.
Star Olivia Hussey (Chris Walters) hated the shoot and was terrified of the Australian bush and its wildlife. She later wrote about the film in her 2018 memoir The Girl on the Balcony.
Hussey was meant to appear topless in a shower scene but asked for a body double. In her memoir she admitted that after seeing the result she wished she'd done it herself.
The nude extras in the film's group shower scene came from a local hippie commune near the Cairns shoot.
Moria's review notes star Steve Railsback (Paul Anders) has claimed that during the troubled production, the producers spent their time at the racetrack while the budget was being cut.
Trenchard-Smith's tongue-in-cheek approach: with prosthetics scarce and money short, he leaned into splatter, reasoning that 'blood is cheap.'
The sadistic Camp Master is named Charles Thatcher, played by Michael Craig. The UK video release was retitled Blood Camp Thatcher, in the Margaret Thatcher era.
Executive producer David Hemmings shot second-unit scenes and clashed with director Brian Trenchard-Smith, who says he once poured beer on Hemmings' head after being mocked in front of his family.
Hemmings co-founded Hemdale, which later made The Terminator (1984) and the Best Picture winners Platoon (1986) and The Last Emperor (1987).
Steve Railsback (Paul Anders) prepared to play Charles Manson in Helter Skelter (1976) by locking himself in a closet for two hours a day.
Co-star Michael Craig wrote in his memoirs that Steve Railsback's method acting on this shoot annoyed him greatly. Trenchard-Smith has also called Railsback 'difficult'.
A major investor pulled out two weeks before the cameras rolled, taking about $700,000 from a $3.2 million budget. The first 15 script pages and a helicopter chase were dropped.
A helicopter-pilot role was written for Australian TV legend Graham Kennedy. The sides couldn't agree terms, so the plot function was reassigned to other characters.
Lynda Stoner (Rita Daniels), a long-time animal-rights campaigner, refused to cut open a real dead fish, so the effects team rushed out a fake one.
Lynda Stoner had been promised no nudity. On set she was pressured, compromised with a back shot, and says she has always regretted it.
Olivia Hussey was Franco Zeffirelli's Juliet in Romeo and Juliet (1968) and the heroine of the slasher Black Christmas (1974). She turned down Fatal Attraction over its boiled-rabbit scene.
Some Australian critics thought Turkey Shoot had ended director Brian Trenchard-Smith's career. His next film, BMX Bandits (1983), with a young Nicole Kidman, was well received.
Director Brian Trenchard-Smith also made Stunt Rock (1978), BMX Bandits (1983) and Dead End Drive-In (1986), all key titles of the Ozploitation boom.
For the gag where a villain's buggy shovel slices a man in half, the crew stuffed suspended trousers with leftover sausage, steak and ketchup. Prosthetics were scarce, and 'blood is cheap.'
Carmen Duncan (Jennifer) was an AFI Award nominee for Harlequin (1980). She later played Iris Wheeler on the US soap Another World from 1988 to 1994.
Time Out said the film 'makes modern day grindhouse imitations such as Machete and Planet Terror seem like anaemic shadows in comparison.'
Australian critic David Stratton called it 'a catalogue of sickening horrors' and said the actors 'should have been ashamed for appearing in such trash.'
Despite the savage reviews, director Brian Trenchard-Smith says Turkey Shoot broke box-office records at some Australian drive-ins.
In the US it was released as Escape 2000 in 1983. New World Pictures sent out a less-cut print, and the MPAA threatened to ban the film unless the heavily cut R-rated version alone was shown.
To promote it in London, the distributor mailed critics rotting chicken feet with their press-screening invitations. It still set a house record at the Warner West End 2 despite a blizzard.
Richard Scheib of Moria gave it one star, saying the gore lacks the snap of The Evil Dead. He notes a poll once named it the worst Australian film ever made, and prefers Dead-End Drive-In.
The film was banned in Scandinavia for years. Its poster there reportedly made actor Roger Ward (guard chief Ritter) look like a Red Army officer.
Quentin Tarantino is a fan. He dedicated the Sydney screening of Kill Bill: Volume 1 to Turkey Shoot, and the film was featured in the documentary Not Quite Hollywood (2008).
At a 1996 premiere, Quentin Tarantino told director Brian Trenchard-Smith he loved the scene 'where the Guard from Hell beats that girl to death on the parade ground.'
The film was remade in 2014, directed by Jon Hewitt and starring Dominic Purcell and Viva Bianca. Original producer Antony I. Ginnane produced it, and Trenchard-Smith was executive producer.
Filmink called it Australia's 10BA take on The Most Dangerous Game, directed 'with great pace' and featuring 'perhaps Australian cinema's most notable werewolf.'
